boundary_spanning_measures.report_type_note: Peer ratings aggregated across consulting team members rating each individual teammate (median rwg = .80, ICC[1] = .28, ICC[2] = .71).
boundary_spanning_measures.source_quote: Closely following existing research, we measured individual boundary-spanning behavior with six items adapted directly from Ancona and Caldwell's (1992) study and modified to reflect the current consulting team context. Team members rated the degree to which each of their teammates engaged in boundary-spanning behaviors (1, "not at all," to 5, "to a very great extent"). A principal components analysis yielded a single factor (alpha = .86).

non_bs_measures.source_quote: In accordance with role theory, we had all participants rate the extent to which they perceived each of the six boundary-spanning behaviors as an expected part of their responsibilities (1, "not at all," to 5, "to a very great extent"). Principal components analysis yielded a single factor (alpha = .86).

We measured boundary-spanning self-efficacy by asking team members to rate their confidence in their ability to successfully engage in a variety of boundary-spanning behaviors. Scale items were based in part upon Parker's (1998) role breadth self-efficacy scale, which asks respondents to rate how confident they feel about contacting individuals outside of their own work units. Eight items were rated on a five-point disagree/agree Likert scale, and principal components analysis yielded a single factor (alpha = .92).

Previous research has shown effects among demographic attributes and employee attitudes and behaviors (Williams & O'Reilly, 1998). Consequently, we included Asian ethnicity (1, "Asian," and 0, "other"), and GMAT score (a continuous score) as controls when predicting individual boundary-spanning behavior.
